# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) has become a cornerstone of sudden cardiac death prevention in patients at risk for life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias [1]. Conventional transvenous ICDs (TV-ICDs), however, are associated with acute and chronic complications related to the intravascular and intracardiac placement of leads, including lead fracture, venous occlusion, and systemic infection requiring complex lead extraction [2,3]. The subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was developed to circumvent these lead-related complications by positioning both the pulse generator and the sensing/defibrillation lead entirely outside the thoracic cavity and vasculature [4]. This review summarizes the rationale, evidence base, clinical performance, limitations, and future directions of the S-ICD.

## Device Design and Rationale

The S-ICD system consists of a pulse generator implanted in a lateral pocket near the left mid-axillary line and a parasternal subcutaneous electrode [4,5]. Because the lead does not contact the heart, the device cannot provide bradycardia pacing, antitachycardia pacing (ATP), or cardiac resynchronization therapy [5]. Sensing relies on subcutaneous electrogram vectors that resemble surface electrocardiograms, and appropriate candidates undergo preimplant screening to confirm an acceptable sensing vector [6]. Early feasibility work demonstrated that an entirely subcutaneous system could reliably detect and terminate induced ventricular fibrillation [4].

## Clinical Evidence

The pivotal IDE study and the EFFORTLESS registry established early safety and efficacy, demonstrating high rates of successful conversion of induced and spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias [7,8]. Pooled analyses of these cohorts confirmed acceptable complication rates and effective arrhythmia termination over intermediate follow-up [9]. The PRAETORIAN trial was the first randomized controlled comparison of S-ICD and TV-ICD in patients without a pacing indication; it demonstrated noninferiority of the S-ICD for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [10]. Notably, the S-ICD group had fewer lead-related complications but more inappropriate shocks attributable to oversensing in early experience [10,11].

The UNTOUCHED study specifically evaluated inappropriate shock rates in a primary-prevention population with reduced ejection fraction using contemporary programming, reporting markedly lower inappropriate shock rates than historical cohorts, largely due to dual-zone programming and improved discrimination algorithms [12]. Registry data have continued to support favorable long-term performance across diverse populations [13,14].

## Patient Selection

The S-ICD is particularly attractive for younger patients, those with prior device infections, patients with limited venous access, and those at higher risk of bacteremia, such as hemodialysis patients [15,16]. It is also favored in patients with channelopathies and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy who do not require pacing [17,18]. Conversely, the device is unsuitable for patients requiring bradycardia pacing, ATP for monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, or resynchronization [5,19]. Preimplant electrocardiographic screening remains essential, as a proportion of patients—particularly those with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy—fail screening due to high T-wave amplitudes that predispose to oversensing [6,18].

## Complications and Limitations

The principal limitations of the S-ICD are inappropriate shocks from T-wave oversensing, the absence of pacing capabilities, and higher defibrillation energy requirements compared with transvenous systems [11,12,20]. Infections tend to remain localized and rarely involve the bloodstream, simplifying management relative to transvenous lead infections [21,22]. Device-related discomfort and erosion at the generator pocket have been reported, prompting refinements in implant technique such as the intermuscular two-incision approach, which improves cosmesis and reduces complications [23,24]. Defibrillation testing at implantation remains common, though its necessity is increasingly debated [25].

## Technological Evolution

A major limitation—the inability to deliver ATP—has driven development of the modular cardiac rhythm management system, which combines an S-ICD with a leadless pacemaker capable of communicating to deliver ATP and bradycardia pacing [26]. The MODULAR ATP trial demonstrated the feasibility and safety of this integrated approach [27]. Iterative improvements in sensing algorithms, including the SMART Pass filter, have substantially reduced oversensing and inappropriate therapies [28]. Continued miniaturization and battery longevity improvements have enhanced device acceptability [29].

## Conclusion

The S-ICD represents an important advance in defibrillation therapy, offering effective protection against sudden cardiac death while avoiding the vascular and lead-related complications of transvenous systems [10,30]. Randomized and registry evidence supports its noninferiority for appropriately selected patients, and ongoing technological innovations—particularly leadless pacing integration—are addressing its principal limitations [27,30]. As selection criteria and programming continue to mature, the S-ICD is poised to assume an expanding role in the management of patients at risk of sudden cardiac death.
